blocks.x: I'll make a note that the date is May the 31st, 1961, and we're interviewing Rudolph. How do you pronounce your last name? Bollier. Bollier. B-E-A-U-L-I-E-U. L-I-E-U. Because there's several names similar to that, and they're all spelled a little different. I saw another way to spell it yesterday in the paper. I was thinking about you then. Do you have any middle name? Peter. Peter. And your first name Rudolph. Is it a ... ...

Well how do you spell his first name? We're asking about his last name. Is it just... A-R-N-O-L-D. A-R-N-O-L-D. Uh-huh. So I wondered if it was some sort of a French pronunciation. Some of them like... That's right. Sometimes they, like the restaurant up here, Arno's restaurant. Yeah, that's right. They leave off the L-D on the end. That's...
Let me just send it as...
Let's leave it here for a minute. We might think something else to ask about him. Um...
You say that he was very good friends with Jim Noon. Very good friends. Can you tell us anything about Jim Noon?
Jim Noon? I didn't know him so well. No more to see him around the house, you know. But it was his personal friend.
What did he play, Jim Noon?
Jim Noon played clarinet.
Clarinet.

Oh, yeah. He was, I think, if I'm not mistaken, I believe he's a relation to... What is it about it's called? D-Booking D I hadn't started yet. But I know them well though, you know, from coming around the house and all that. And my brother was a jolly fella, you know, I'd be on the street with him. He'd make me meet him, make me acquainted with him. That's how I know them.
Can you remember what type of a person Jimmy Newton was? Was he tall or short or thin or fat?
Yeah, he was short and fat.
Short and fat?
Something just on the heart of this fella.
About Arnaud? Yeah. Yeah. And was he a son of a jolly fella, you'd say?

My brother was. We'd take to meet all those different fellas. That's how I know them. What's the heck I couldn't get on? Huh? What'd he say then? I say he was a jolly fella, all the time joking and caring about. Your brother. And I'd be on the street with him, let me meet them fellas to see what he knows. That's how I know plenty of them to him. And then going around different dances, you know. Yeah. I got a hold of to know plenty of them. Yeah. And different places he'd be playing, come sit around, you know. He'd make me know. I don't guess he'd know that I was going to ever be a drummer. I don't think he'd know that. He might have had a nod, he might have kept it to himself.
Yeah. I don't believe he'd know. Is this the set of drums you learned on, you think? That same little, looks like a wooden... It could've been. It could've been. You were telling about...
Because he... I changed drums plenty, but he didn't.
Yeah, he kept the same one.
Kept the same one.
You mentioned when the con place opened up on Barone Street.

On Barone Street. What kind did they sell? They sold Ludwig drums. Ludwig. Now, I was... I got in with them somewhere and another. I was well known with them. And, uh... They began to lend me drums. You see, like if I go... I tell them I want to buy a set of drums. But use this set today to see how it'll work out.
Yeah.

And let me go off with that set. I'd bring it back. I'd try out another set like that. Oh, it was very nice for that. And... And... Yeah. I must've tried out about three or four different sets around there. Yes, indeed. And I bought a set off of them thereafter. Finally bought a set. I think I lost about... About three or four sets of drums. I got in tough luck and I pawned them by Goebel Brothers on the record. Oh, yeah. And I lost them. I got out of work, you know. And, uh... I lost my drums. About three or four sets.
Yeah. Sure.

I bought a bass drum. I brought it home. It had a big fireplace, something like this. Mm-hmm. And, uh... I hadn't used it. Just bought it. From CG Conn. Bring it home. No, Warline I bought that in front. Set it in front of the fireplace. They had some dust in there somewhere or not. Might have swept dust in there, you know. And... I come in, I lit the... They had lamps. We had lamps. It didn't have no electric.
Yeah, it was ordinary lamp.

Load the... Uh, lit that, uh, electric lamp. And show them to match it at dust. And... You puffed up. Well, no. I went on out. Closed the door. When I come back, I notice a lot of smoke in there. Yeah. So, I opened the door right away, you know. And when I got in, the drum was on fire. It didn't burn. I just had bought it. Yeah, you got it. And put it in front of it. And, uh... I didn't... They claim I didn't have any shoot at the house because I just had bought it. Uh, it wasn't an shoot yet, so I had to pay for it.
Yeah.
Brand new drum.
Yeah.
Didn't use it once. Not even practice all the time.
The shell and everything burned?
Shell and everything went. Oh.
Yes. Well, uh... I guess that skin would go quick, but it's funny the shell would burn that fast.
Actually, I don't know how long it's been, but I've been in that first union. Remember when I had that colored union? I think there was a meeting up around Iberville Street somewhere.
Was that when Robichaud helped?
I believe some, you know... I believe some, you know... What is the problem that got killed? Gahir?
Yes, I've heard of him.
Well, uh... I believe he got some of that money. They broke up. I hadn't got out of it then. And they broke up and they wiped that money between themselves. That's why. Who did? Huh?
Who did that?
The officers? I don't know. I don't know who did. That's what I heard. It got in the wind somehow and I got a hold of that. And said the money that was left, they wiped it up between them.
Yeah, Jim.
Now, this, then a long time after, they had, we worked all the dances up and they made up another union. Well, that's the one I'm in now.
Yeah.
That must prove a good satisfaction.
Yeah. It's national all over the country, I guess.
Uh... Well, since I've been in there, it looks like things have been going real good so far. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Continue. Uh... Yeah.
Some good officers now. Yeah. What about old man Contrell? Speaking of the president, his father was a drummer. Do you remember much about him? Sure. That was his daddy? Yeah.
That's something I didn't know.
You didn't know that?
Uh... Listen. Old man Contrell was living on this side of the street. I'm living on this side of the street. Oh, really? A big, tall fella, brown skin. He was playing with Nanga Perez's brass band.
Yeah, I knew he played.

And, uh... Yeah, that's right. That's the name, all right? I can't recall his first name, but that's his name. He's a big, tall fella. And he could play with some drums. Well, I've heard. Yes, sir. You've heard. I'm telling you, you can believe me. I can tell you all those that could play and all those that couldn't play.
Who were your favorite drummers? I suppose your brother would be one of them, but who else?

No, I wouldn't say that. You wouldn't rank him as the best or anything then, huh? No, he's a good drummer because he's a regular nightclub man, you know? Yeah. And, uh... Because he played with all the different fellas I'm telling you about. Jimmy Noon. Uh... Uh... Alvin Nicholas. And I wouldn't say Bonabigo because Bonabigo had come in on the last.
He was just learning, I guess, huh?

Yeah, and, uh... He learned. He learned. And when he got a good foothold, then he left away from here. That's when he was a musician and when he left here. Yeah. I don't know... Somebody told me he was playing with Duke, was it?
Well, yeah. He played with him, I think, 13 years. Wow. A long time. He just quit him about 1940. He went with him in the 20s.
Well that's when he got to be a musician when he left here. He wasn't much when he was here in New Orleans.
And he played with Joe Oliver up in Chicago too, I know.

Yeah. Oh, man. Now that's a fella I could play a home. I remember one night I wasn't playing yet. I was just a youngster getting around, you know. And I was standing, he was playing with a big tall fella, who plays violin. I don't know where did he get that tone out of that violin, but did he have some tone? Sweat say it was an electric violin.
It was electric? No, it wasn't.
I swear to say it was.
Oh, yeah.

It was. You could be on the outside like I was listening. Yeah, it was a while. I climbed on top of a beer barrel and I was in the window looking in, you see. Yeah. There were a lot of youngsters in the district then.
What place was that?
On Franklin between Iberville and Canal.
That wouldn't be the 25s.
25, that's right. Big 25. And they had a fella by the name. I heard my brother, this fella, tell me his name was Valtu.
Oh, yeah. I've heard that. Professor Vanetta talks about him a lot.

Yeah? Yeah. An old man Valtu. Yeah. Well, I'm telling you. He's down here. That's the one I heard. I was in that one they had Joe Oliver, that old man Valtu. I think they had about five pieces in there. Drums and whatever else they had. I don't know. Because I was peeping in that window like a transom I was looking. I was looking. I stand on top of a beer bell and something else. And the police had come and cracked me.
And I mean I hopped off that thing too quick for a hurry. Yeah.
There's a lot of youngsters around there then, you see. It's a shame.
All you wanted to do was listen to the music then.

That's all. It's a shame. Couldn't it help? Yeah. I was trying to make my wealth, you see. Mm-hmm. And, but there was such a bunch of fellas that looked like they wasn't interested. All they were interested in making that money and that's all. Nothing else behind them. Yeah. Yeah. And so, fool with them kind of guys, I never would get nowhere. And I guess in a band over the river, Red Allen's daddy. Oh yeah. In the brass band. They didn't have ballrooms too much then. They had them little hole in the wall, you know. Yeah. I don't guess I should be talking about it over the river.
No, that's good. That doesn't matter. We talk about everything on these things.
And, uh.
Find out what things were really like in those days. Yeah.

So I got fired at that band because, you see, like we play a funeral and they finish, uh, like say here, you know. You go pay off where that, two, three blocks at that corner. Oh yeah. Uh, so we can buy the liquor, you see what I mean. They had no barroom, you know, that's paying off. They had to go without. Well, I wouldn't buy no liquor. I bought it once or twice and I told them I ain't doing it no more. Because the job wasn't paying that much. And if you had to take and go make four or five dollars, you know, sweat yourself to them. And then I have to go buy a liquor, nothing to come with don't make sense. So I told them I wasn't going to do it no more. And they fired them. Yeah. Get rid of me. And I got fired out about two or three bands on the counter there. And, uh, Kid Howard did me the same thing. Yeah. Yeah. Boy, I don't know what to tell you. And I had lots of work one time. Yeah. I gave all them fellas work. They never fix me up like I fix them up. But I'm living, you know. They never fix me up. Yeah. And, uh, I used to have, uh, this Maison Blanche annex I just opened. I used to work for them, advertise. He said, go and put us up on that second floor up there. And we played for the customers that come in. Right in the stores.
Right in the stores.

Yes sir. And then I had a Petone's, uh, fighting arena, the fifth water athletic club. Every Friday. Where was that? That street? That athletic club on the domain between Decatur and Charlotte. And then I had a, uh, on the downtown side of the bank. Cause it was called the Fifth Water Athletic Club. That was every Friday. I had, uh, Fry's Grocery on Canal and Villeary, Food Store. It was advertised for them. I think it was every Tuesday or Wednesday. And... You got on a truck there? Yeah, on a truck. And, uh, it was filled up pretty good. It was filled up pretty good all the way. Yeah. Different places we'd go play a dance. You see, plenty of bands at that time. You see when the holidays would come along? Mm-hm. And, uh, people would be like crazy around and looking for a band. Yes, please. Now they've got too many bands. Yeah. All of the youngsons. No jobs. All of the youngsons go to school now. They go with their school band and play for these dances for nothing. Mm-hm. And, uh, let's shed a side planet place. I guess so. The music box, they shed a side planet place. Yeah. So that's what a musician can't make a head with. You see when I first started playing, every man is on trade. Musicians played music. Carpenter, he was a carpenter, he stayed in his place, he ain't coming my way. Slater and different other people, they stood on their side. Well that gave me a chance to play music. Musicians played nightclubs and all like that. Well he's filling his arm play. They had work for them. But now the carpenter's is playing music, Slater's, and the, what you call it, people, people working in the market, they're musicians too. Oh you find musicians all over. Now you ain't got no trouble looking for a band. You come at this corner, you don't find a band, go at this corner and get it. But when I was coming, it wasn't like that. You take and have work and have plenty of it. And you could demand your price. You know what people used to tell me? I want you to come over, you don't have to play nothing, just make a game of plenty noise, that's all. Oh I said, no indeed. I said, we don't do that kind of business. And if they wouldn't tell you that, they'd tell you, they wouldn't want to give you a big price. They said, we'll give you plenty of eating drinks. I worked for Sergeant Morrison, Captain Anderson, all them fellas, American Legion, you know. Yeah. Go out on the lake on a picnic. We're going to give you plenty of eating drinks. I said, well Cap, I'll tell you. I said, I eat and drink plenty at my house. Well sometime I might go to jail, we'll get you out. I said, I don't go to no jail. I said, because I'm a man, I stay to myself, I don't go look for no trouble. And if I see trouble and I try to get out the way from you, of course anybody can get in trouble. Yeah, that's right, sometime. But I said, I don't believe you, I'll be able to cash back on you. I said, the offers you give me, I said, I got to have my money, so I paid a mendo. So, let's forget about the eating and drinking. Well I'll play that job. You remember when Captain Anderson fell off that camp at the lake? I don't remember about that, no.
I wasn't there then.

I was playing on a job when he fell back off the camp and broke his leg. Really? Sergeant Morris, another one, he wanted to throw my money in the canal when I finished playing. Well there's always a good fellow in the crowd. I said, I come along and he said, why don't you have to invite them boys and play it all day for you? What you want to throw that money on in that lake? Put them caps on the water. If you'd thrown it down in the lake, you could look right down there, watch how clear that water was. You could look right down that water and see it. I've seen the water that's clear out there now, sometimes. It's going to make you die for him, huh?
Huh? It's going to make you die in the water for him.

Yeah, no you didn't have to die. You just have to come down on that step that's going in the water. Who wanted to do that? You didn't work for that money, it was yours. And so one good fellow come along, oh get them people that money, let them go home. Well, he finally paid off.
That was who did that? That was Sergeant Morris.
He wanted to do it, he didn't do anything.
That was a police force. Huh? On the police force. How did he relate to that? A sergeant? Was he a sergeant in the army?
No, no. City police. City police.
Yeah.

And we had plenty of messages, man. We went out in the country and played music. I went with Kid Howard one time. And I had said I never was going out there no more. Out in Grand Isle. Oh yeah. And then that other place down around Michelle Beach.
Out at West End? No, no.

Down that way? Not that out in Semonaut Parish. Oh no, I don't know. There's never been down there much. There's Delacro Island. Delacro Island, that's it. Is that it? Yeah. I seen them people fight down there so that it was scary to look at them. It was cold. It was cold and raining. Ice fall on the ground. They fight and they cut up one another and roll all underneath the cars and everything. You heard that time when they whip up Papa Celestad's band? No, nobody ever told us that. Yeah, the whip up Papa Celestad's band. Down at Delacro Island? Down at Delacro Island. Down at the top of each car. They paid for that, they told me. After that they got the... Are they all drunk or something? Oh they did. They'd never be sober. Yeah. Not down there. And so I said I was never going out there no more. So some fellas, they had me to go down there. They told me I was going to Shell Beach. After I noticed the road you were taking, I said, Hey man, you're not going to Shell Beach. Oh, I didn't want to tell you because I know you wasn't going to go down there. And we needed a drummer tonight. And everything was going to come out all right. When the girls down there, they hit Kid Howard. They just kept the truck and bottles and things. And finally, they hit the bass player. Sidney Brown. Oh yeah. He hit Sidney Brown too. So I said, Y'all fellas are going to go and tell the man that what's happening. I said, Because I don't want to get in no trouble out here. So finally they reported to the man. He said, There ain't nothing going to happen to y'all. I said, Well listen mister. I said, Ain't nothing going to happen. You're going to be here and we hit that road and they make a roadblock and we can't go no further. Something will happen. So he said, You boy at home. He said, Ain't nothing going to happen. Well sure enough, Nothing didn't happen. But I said, If it didn't happen that time, It's not going to happen because I ain't going down there to move. And I never did go down there either. That was my last trip down there. No way.
Was there a picnic ground there or something?
No.
Dance hall.

Dance hall. There's a two or three dance hall down there. Now there's a fellow by the name of Freddie Faber. He's a drummer too. Or he's trying to be one of the two. But he broke my drum one night. And of course it didn't amount to much. But the next time I went down there I said, Listen Mr. Freddie, I said, I can't afford to be buying drum heads. I said, You take and let me hold a five dollar bill and you can go ahead and break them. I can buy some more. But I said, Me digging down my pocket, I said, That ain't no boy. Now they say he was a bad fellow. But I didn't mind talking man for my rights. And he gave him a five dollar bill and the first stroke he made, the stick went in the drum. He got up. But it was too late for him to get up. Then he hadn't broken. The first stroke he made. And the way he used to bang on them cymbals was the shit. And so I went home with these five dollars that night. I got two heads for that five dollar bill. Bottom and the top, it was all at the top of that rope. Next time I went down there, same old thing, give him a five dollar bill. He didn't break no that night, but I gave him his five dollar bill. When I went down there again, he said he didn't take no chance. I said, well that's one way of getting rid of him. He broke that when he paid for that one right after that. Yeah. Now, since then I haven't went. They beat up Papa Celeste. That was before he died.
Did they beat up the whole band or just the whole band? The whole band. Well how long ago would that be? After the war?

Before the war? Oh, that wasn't too long ago. Let me see what Papa Celeste there. Before he went in that nightclub on Bourbon Street. Before that. That was before that. Yeah. And this fellow was playing banjo. What's this guy play all them rock and roll numbers? I don't know.
What did he do? Well I think that was Fats Domino now.
Fats Domino. That's why his nephew plays the guitar. Oh yeah.
He was playing with Papa Celeste there then. Yeah. What's his name?

Well they tore it on top of his car. You had one of them, I forget the name of the cars. I don't know how they tore it all the time. They cut it off. Yeah. Well I believe they paid for it because they made a charge against him or something. And they had to face code for it. And whoever it was, they made him pay for it. Yeah, they upped it. But they couldn't take that whipping off of them though. No. And after they'd tell me they whipped Howard. That's the reason why I didn't want to go that way anymore. After I heard all that I said well I ain't going to give them the opportunity to go to me now. No. Stay out of there. Maybe I might get it worse than them. Yeah. And I quit from that time on.
Must have been a rough crowd out there.

There be a rough crowd all the time. Them fellas from here goes over there to the dancers. Them guys over there, see them feeling aching with them girls or something. They all like that. They all make up a crowd, you see. And I'm sorry for the guy who would be. Yeah. They beat him up something terrible. The sheriff that night said, nobody interfere. Leave him fight. They want to fight, leave him fight. And they fit in a roller in the automobile and all that water and ice. I said I already see it's him and me. Yeah. They fight terrible. The sheriff didn't even stop. No he didn't stop. There's one thing I wanted to ask you. You mentioned the name Val-to. It sounds like a French name.
How do you spell that name? I wouldn't know. I heard them call the name Val-to. I know it starts with a V. It might be. Now it could be Bal-to too. It wouldn't have to be Val-to. It could be Bal-to.

Some of those French names start with F when they pronounce it V too. Yeah. Like I'm thinking of a clarinetist up in Chicago, Val-e-Difo. Val-e-Difo. Val-e-Difo. Vo. Something they call it Faux and some V-e-difo. I think sometimes those names . Well look at this story . It should be Val-to . It should be Val-to .

It should be Val-to . start with the F and they pronounce it V too. Yeah. Like I'm thinking of a clarinetist up in Chicago, Valle de Vaux. Valle de Vaux. Well no I mean his last name though. Vaux, something they call Vaux and something Vaux. I think sometimes those names... Well look at this Scott,
it's not telling you about it. Anon Matoie. Yeah. But some people call him Matoie.

Yeah. Anon Matoie. Oh and we talked to his daughter and his widow too, they're still living, and we asked his daughter how to pronounce it and she said we call it Matoie. Yeah. Like it's spelled in English T-O-Y-E-R. Matoie. Like a toy. That's right.

Because I know another father, I don't know if he's related to them, Sidney Matoie. He lives up here in a bar room somewhere up around in Sallahan or Claiborne, somewhere up around town. And I don't know if he's in relation to them or not. He's a good friend with my brother too. Mm-hmm. Oh, there's lots of things I can tell you. You gotta help me out. Yeah. I think I forgot you know. And. I was going to mention once more about
your brother. His hat's got the Eagle Band cap. Who? Your brother Arnold. Yeah. Would that Eagle Band be both a brass band and a dance band? They used to play in brass band,

but that was a string band. That was a string band? Yeah. I think that was a six piece or a seven piece orchestra. You see after they started using that saxophone they used seven pieces. Yeah. Because whoever was playing clarinet they didn't want to find or get rid of them and then started away. So what they did they kept the clarinet and they used clarinet and saxophone
and the wolf on the band. Do you remember who else was in the band when your brother was in it? My brother used to change your arms so much.
Yeah, I did. Yeah, they never kept a steady band all the time. There was always something confused and one fellow would quit or they'd fire somebody if he wasn't right and get somebody
else. When you say a string band, what would be the usual instruments in a string band?

Why they call it a string band? That drum, piano, guitar and bass. So this, that trumpet and trombone was the only two, you know what I mean, in sight. The rest was all string instruments. So they used to call it a string band. And violin? Yeah, they used to use violin too. See like Piron? Yeah. Oh, Piron had a band mostly string instruments. He used to use violinists. Then they had guitar, he had piano and bass. That's a lot of string instruments in a band. Yeah, that's right. And with drums, you know. And with drums, you couldn't say well, they would consider string anyhow.
More like a string instrument. Yeah.

You think because of the snares or why do they call it a string? Not because it was a bass, I mean a bass drum in it or a drum, that it couldn't play soft. Yeah. You could use a drum just like you, and use it that you could hear all about the instrument. I go as to sign up a job on Audubon Street one day. And lady called me up. I goes up there to see her. And I mentioned to her about how many pieces I had in the band. And I began to call them out. When I say drums, she liked to jump out of her clothes. I said, oh, no indeed. I said, what's the matter, lady? She said, well, I wouldn't have that up in here. I said, well, I'm the drummer. And you called me. And I said, you wouldn't want to give all them fellas a job and shet myself out of that. Oh, no, she said, but I wouldn't want no drums. I said, now, lady, I tell you what I'm going to do. You hire the band. Just hire the band. And if you don't like the drum, when we come up here at night, stop the band. Just keep the rest of the instrument you want to keep, and everything will come out all right. I ain't going to force you to take the drum. But I'm the manager of my band, and I'm the drummer. And I'm not going to shit myself out of a piece of bread to help the other guy. So I said, if you don't like it that night, I won't play. You know what that lady told her that night? When I was playing a band, she come to me, she said, Mr., I ain't never know the drum could play that soft. Well, I mean, she heard all the other instruments. And I never used no jazz sticks, no. Use the regular sticks. Regular sticks. Regular sticks. But I forgot to say it myself, I'm very light on drums. And I ain't never had no complaints since I've been playing with a different band. As Nene Strapania, I went on his job one night at the Moulin Rouge at the West End. Oh yeah. And he was playing with Papa. And I went out there and the fellas said, man, I wish they'd send you at you all the time. Is he a pretty noisy drummer? No, but they claim I'm working better than him. So, all right. But I always would go on the job with an excuse. You know, before I start playing, I would want to find out how they work, you know, so I could work with them like they wanted me. And everybody, I'm not bragging on myself, but everybody I work with, like the time of music up there. See, I keep such good time. I don't try to make no whole lot of explosion like any other fella. I would make some time what I can, what I can't. I leave it alone. If I think I'm a spoiled something, I don't fool with them. And I always keep good time. That's my particular way of doing it.

How big a drum set do you usually have? Or did you like to use? What else did you use besides your snare drum and bass drum? And how many cymbals? I used two cymbals. And I got my set here. If you'd like to see it, I should. If it's not in trouble, you can just tell us about it. Maybe you'd not bother to get it out. Did you have a wood block?

I had everything. I work in a cabaret out on Decatur Street. And I had everything. Wood blocks, bells, I got all in here. Cowbells? Yeah. How many of those did you use? Four. Four of them. Four-carter belly, wood blocks. I had triangles. I had two triangles. And two Tom-Toms. And I want to sell an instrument because I don't know what I'll be able to play again. If you want to keep it a while, then you can play again. Yeah. Did you ever use a ratchet? A who? A ratchet? Yeah. I'd print you everything you could mention because every time something new come out and I'd go around the music store and tell them about it, buy it.
I wanted to ask you, did you notice any difference when you changed from the overhead pedal to the under?
Well, I think the floor pedal was more, you get a more force stage, you know, than that overhead. That's one thing about it. Yeah, and quick action.
Oh, you think it's quick action?

Yeah. I think it gives you quick action. And you see, I don't beat like some fellas with my heels to the floor, you see. I just beat with my tiptoes. My foot beat completely on the floor. You lift your whole leg up. My whole leg is, this is my, this is my tools.
Yeah.

I don't see many fellas beat like that. There was one fella, Roy, they call him, used to live uptown, he used to play with Chris Kelly's band. And he was one fella that I saw do that. And I kept that up. But I don't, I don't see fellas beat like that. I can't beat with my foot on the ground. I can, you know what I mean? But I don't give quick action like, I just beat with my toes.
I'm just about out of this reel here if you feel like going another half hour. I can go as long as you want to go. Alright, unless you're worn out. We don't want to make you get tired. Tired?
Not keeping you from your supper, are we? Huh? Not keeping you from your supper?

No, indeed. I don't. Y'all want a cold drink? I don't believe so unless you do that. Thank you very much. We just stopped on the way over and had some root beer. I wonder what happened to Harold. He must be pulling out his teeth. Oh. Oh. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Spelling of the name Beaulieu and his brother Arnold
segments.summary: Opening date note and discussion of how Beaulieu's name and his brother Arnold's name are spelled and pronounced.

segments.title: Brother's friend Jimmie Noone and meeting musicians through his brother
segments.summary: Rudolph recalls clarinetist Jimmie Noone as his brother's friend and says he came to know many musicians by going around with his brother to dances and jobs.

segments.title: His brother's drum set and changing his own drums
segments.summary: Discussion of the drums he learned on; his brother kept the same set while he changed drums often.

segments.title: Trying and buying Ludwig drums, pawning sets, and a new bass drum burned
segments.summary: A music store lent him sets of Ludwig drums to try; he lost several sets to pawn and tells how a brand-new bass drum caught fire by the fireplace.

segments.title: The first colored musicians' union and the later one
segments.summary: He recalls the first colored union breaking up with its money allegedly divided by the officers, and the later union he now belongs to.

segments.title: Old man Cottrell, drummer in a brass band
segments.summary: He remembers Cottrell as a big tall neighbor who played drums in a brass band.

segments.title: Favorite drummers, his brother, and Barney Bigard
segments.summary: He rates his brother as a good nightclub drummer and says Barney Bigard only became a musician after leaving New Orleans for Duke Ellington.

segments.title: Peeping into the 25 Club to hear Joe Oliver as a boy
segments.summary: As a youngster he climbed on a beer barrel to listen at the window of the 25 club on Franklin Street, where Joe Oliver played, until the police chased him.

segments.title: Getting fired from a brass band over buying liquor after funerals
segments.summary: He was fired from a brass band and other bands for refusing to pay for liquor after funerals, and says Kid Howard did the same to him.

segments.title: Advertising jobs, plentiful work then, and demanding his price
segments.summary: He describes playing in store advertising and athletic club jobs, how musicians used to be only musicians, and insisting on pay instead of food and drink.

segments.title: Policeman who wanted to throw his pay into the lake
segments.summary: At a lake picnic job a city police sergeant tried to withhold or throw away the band's money until another man intervened.

segments.title: Dangerous dance jobs at Delacroix Island
segments.summary: He describes brawling crowds at Delacroix Island, a trick played to get him on the job with Kid Howard and Sidney Brown, and why he never went back.

segments.title: Freddie Faber breaking his drumheads
segments.summary: A drummer broke his drumheads, so Rudolph made him pay five dollars in advance.

segments.title: Papa Celestin's band beaten up at Delacroix Island
segments.summary: He recounts the band of Papa Celestin being beaten, a rough crowd, and the sheriff refusing to stop the fighting.

segments.title: Pronouncing French names: Valteau, Matoie
segments.summary: The interviewers and Rudolph discuss spelling and pronunciation of French names such as Val-to and Matoie, and Sidney Matoie.

segments.title: The Eagle Band as a string band
segments.summary: His brother played in the Eagle Band, a six or seven piece string band that added saxophone, with frequent personnel changes.

segments.title: What a string band was, and Piron's band
segments.summary: He explains why bands with piano, guitar, bass and violin were called string bands, citing Piron.

segments.title: Playing drums softly and a woman who refused a drummer
segments.summary: He tells of a woman who hated drums until she heard how softly he played, and describes his light touch and steady time, including filling in for another drummer at the Moulin Rouge.

segments.title: His drum set, cowbells, and floor pedal technique
segments.summary: He lists the cymbals, blocks, cowbells and tom-toms he used, prefers the floor pedal, and describes beating with his toes like the drummer Roy.

segments.title: End of the reel and pleasantries
segments.summary: The interviewer notes the reel is nearly out and the group chats before stopping.
